source_reference: Mishneh Torah, Foundations of the Torah 1:1-6
english_source_translation: Mishneh Torah, Foundations of the Torah 1:1–6: “The foundation of all foundations and the pillar of wisdom is to know that there is a First Being Who brought every existing thing into being. All beings of heaven and earth, and everything between them, exist only through the truth of His existence... The knowledge of this matter is a positive commandment, as it is said: 'I am the Lord your God' (Exodus 20:2). And whoever entertains the thought that there is another deity besides this transgresses a negative commandment, as it is said: 'You shall have no other gods before Me' (Exodus 20:3), and denies the fundamental principle upon which everything depends.”

And we recite: “The soul You gave within me is pure” (Berakhot 60b), which implies even in the present moment; and that is because the inception of evil is in the heart, as written in chapter HaRoeh (ibid. 61a): that the evil inclination sits upon the portals of the heart.…” In Likkutei Maamarim, Upon Completion of Talmud 5 (sharing the proof-text Sanhedrin 90a, Avodah Zarah 17a), Rav Tzadok develops the complementary dimension of this principle, illuminating how Mishneh Torah, Foundations of the Torah 1:1-6 anchors the inner service of the heart in Sefer HaZikhronot.

english_source_translation: Sefer Mitzvot Katan (Semak) §1: “Indeed, the Holy One, blessed be He, guides the entire universe with the breath of His mouth, and He brought us out of Egypt and performed all the wonders for us; not even a person's finger is bruised below unless it is proclaimed concerning him from Above, as it is said: 'A man's steps are established by the Lord' (Psalms 37:23). Upon this rests the teaching of the Sages that at the hour of judgment after death a person is asked, 'Did you hope for salvation?'—for just as I desire that you believe in Me that I brought you out of Egypt, so too I desire that you believe in Me that I am the Lord your God and that I am destined to gather you and save you.”
kisvei_rav_tzadok_parallel: Kisvei Rav Tzadok Parallel — Peri Tzadik, Bereshit 1:2: “For within fear there is the fear of God (yirat Elohim), which is the lower dread of retribution, and this category of fear is not the ultimate purpose of Creation, as we find even concerning the inhabitants of Nineveh: 'and they covered themselves with sackcloth, etc., who knows, He may turn, etc.,' where it was exclusively the fear of punishment alone, as it is stated: 'and turn away from His fierce anger, that we perish not.…” In Peri Tzadik, Bereshit 1:2 (sharing the proof-text Berakhot 28b, Isaiah 6:3), Rav Tzadok develops the complementary dimension of this principle, illuminating how Sefer Mitzvot Katan 1 anchors the inner service of the heart in Sefer HaZikhronot.

source_reference: Duties of the Heart, Gate of Trust, Introduction
english_source_translation: Chovot HaLevavot (Duties of the Heart), Sha'ar HaBitachon, Introduction: “It is told of one of the ascetics that at the beginning of his abstinence he traveled to a distant land to seek his livelihood, where he encountered a fire-worshipper who asked him whom he served. The ascetic replied: 'I serve the Creator, the Almighty, the Sustainer, beside Whom there is none.' The magus said to him: 'Your action contradicts your words! If He truly sustained you in your hometown just as He sustains you here, you would not have troubled yourself to journey to a distant land.' The ascetic's argument was silenced; he returned to his town and accepted upon himself complete trust in God from that time onward.”

english_source_translation: Sotah 49a: “Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua: From the day the Temple was destroyed, there is no day without a curse, the dew has not descended for blessing, and the flavor of fruit has been taken away. Rava said: Every single day its curse is more severe than that of the day before, as it is stated: 'In the morning you shall say, Would that it were evening! and in the evening you shall say, Would that it were morning!' (Deuteronomy 28:67).”

english_source_translation: Bava Kamma 9b: “If we say it means that one should spend up to one-third of his estate to perform a mitzva, but if that is so, and if it happened to him that he became obligated in three mitzvot at the same time, should he give his entire estate away in order to fulfill those mitzvot? One is certainly not required to do so. Rather, what Rabbi Zeira said is that for the embellishment of the performance of a mitzva, e.g., to purchase a more beautiful item used in the performance of a mitzva, one should spend up to one-third more than the cost of the standard item used to perform the mitzva. Rav Ashi raises a dilemma: How is this one-third calculated? Is it one-third from within, i.e.…”

english_source_translation: Bava Metzia 62a: ““And your brother shall live with you” (Leviticus 25:36), from which it is derived: Return the interest to him so that he may live. The Gemara asks: And Rabbi Yoḥanan, what does he do with this verse: “And your brother shall live with you”? The Gemara answers: He requires the verse for that which is taught in a baraita: If two people were walking on a desolate path and there was a jug [kiton] of water in the possession of one of them, and the situation was such that if both drink from the jug, both will die, as there is not enough water, but if only one of them drinks, he will reach a settled area, there is a dispute as to the halakha. Ben Petora taught: It is preferable that both of them drink and die, and let neither one of them see the death of the other.…”

english_source_translation: Beitzah 16a: “A person’s entire livelihood is allocated to him during the period from Rosh HaShana to Yom Kippur. During that time, as each individual is judged, it is decreed exactly how much money he will earn for all his expenditures of the coming year, except for expenditures for Shabbatot, and expenditures for Festivals, and expenditures for the school fees of his sons’ Torah study. In these areas, no exact amount is determined at the beginning of the year; rather, if he reduced the amount he spends for these purposes, his income is reduced and he earns that much less money in that year, and if he increased his expenditures in these areas, his income is increased to ensure that he can cover the expense.…”

english_source_translation: Sotah 48b: “'From the time the Temple was destroyed, men of faith (anshei amanah) ceased.' Rabbi Yitzchak said: These are people who place their trust in the Holy One, blessed be He, as it was taught: Rabbi Eliezer the Great says: Whoever has bread in his basket and says, 'What shall I eat tomorrow?' is none other than of little faith (miketanei amanah). And Rabbi Elazar said: What is the meaning of 'For who has despised the day of small things?' (Zechariah 4:10)—what caused the tables of the righteous to be diminished in the World to Come? The smallness of faith that was in them, in that they did not trust wholly in the Holy One, blessed be He.”

english_source_translation: Berakhot 24b: “and if he was stung by a louse, he may feel for it and remove it with his garment, but he would not wrap himself in his prayer shawl if it fell during prayer. And when he would yawn he would place his hand on his chin so that his open mouth would not be visible. The Gemara raises an objection based on a baraita: One who sounds his voice during his Amida prayer is among those of little faith, as he seems to believe that the Lord cannot hear his prayer when it is uttered silently. One who raises his voice during prayer is considered to be among the false prophets, as they too were wont to cry out and shout to their gods. Furthermore, one who belches and yawns while praying is surely among the uncouth. One who sneezes during his prayer, for him it is a bad omen.…”

english_source_translation: Deuteronomy 8:2–18: “'And you shall remember all the way which the Lord your God has led you these forty years in the wilderness, that He might humble you, to test you... And He humbled you, and suffered you to hunger, and fed you with manna... that He might make you know that man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds out of the mouth of the Lord does man live... Beware lest you forget the Lord your God... and you say in your heart: My power and the might of my hand have gotten me this wealth. But you shall remember the Lord your God, for it is He Who gives you power to get wealth.'”

english_source_translation: Deuteronomy 8: “You shall faithfully observe all the Instruction that I enjoin upon you today, that you may thrive and increase and be able to possess the land that GOD promised on oath to your fathers. Remember the long way that the ETERNAL your God has made you travel in the wilderness these past forty years, in order to test you by hardships to learn what was in your hearts: whether you would keep the commandments or not. [God] subjected you to the hardship of hunger and then gave you manna to eat, which neither you nor your ancestors had ever known, in order to teach you that a human being does not live on bread alone, but that one may live on anything that GOD decrees. The clothes upon you did not wear out, nor did your feet swell these forty years.…”

kisvei_rav_tzadok_parallel: Kisvei Rav Tzadok Parallel — Takanat HaShavin 3:4: “And behold, by the Torah [-law] — though it and all the prophets exhorted regarding teshuvah — nonetheless this does not avail to nullify the words of the Torah: that is, to exempt from court-imposed death and lashes (for a willful sin) and a korban (for an inadvertent one) — even if he repented with his whole heart, in truth.…” In Takanat HaShavin 3:4 (sharing the proof-text Bava Kamma 50a), Rav Tzadok develops the complementary dimension of this principle, illuminating how Deuteronomy 7:9-10 anchors the inner service of the heart in Sefer HaZikhronot.

english_source_translation: Berakhot 63a: “and say as follows: With regard to the Temple Mount, where one is prohibited from wearing shoes, let us derive the prohibition of spitting from the case of shoes. However, with regard to a synagogue, where one is permitted to wear shoes, instead of deriving the law with regard to spitting from the case of shoes and permitting it, derive it from the case of a shortcut, and prohibit it. Rather, Rava said a different reason: The synagogue is like one’s house. Just as one objects to a person using his house as a shortcut, but does not mind spitting and wearing shoes therein, so too in the case of a synagogue, a shortcut is prohibited while spitting and wearing shoes are permitted.…”
kisvei_rav_tzadok_parallel: Kisvei Rav Tzadok Parallel — Tzidkat HaTzadik 128:1: “When a person commits a transgression under the principle of "It is time to work for Hashem; they have made void Your Torah" (Psalms 119:126) or "In all your ways acknowledge Him" (Proverbs 3:6), he nonetheless requires atonement for the transgression he committed, as in that which they taught (Berakhot 31b): a Torah scholar who fasts on Shabbat must sit in a subsequent fast to atone for having fasted on Shabbat; and likewise in Sanhedrin 26b: they reasoned they were performi…” In Tzidkat HaTzadik 128:1 (sharing the proof-text Bava Kamma 50a), Rav Tzadok develops the complementary dimension of this principle, illuminating how Berakhot 63a anchors the inner service of the heart in Sefer HaZikhronot.

english_source_translation: Yoma 9b: “that they deferred the sacrifice of their bird-offerings by women after childbirth; nevertheless, the verse ascribes to them as if they lay with them. These women came to the Tabernacle to sacrifice doves or pigeons as bird-offerings as part of their purification process, which would permit them to engage in sexual relations with their husbands. Eli’s sons delayed the sacrifice of these offerings and thereby delayed the return of these women to their husbands and their fulfillment of the mitzva of procreation. Even though, according to this opinion, Eli’s sons did not actually engage in sexual relations with these women, the verse attributes that degree of severity to their conduct.…”
kisvei_rav_tzadok_parallel: Kisvei Rav Tzadok Parallel — Machshavot Charutz 20:19: “And in its literal sense: recounting his might at the beginning and end was necessary out of dread of the empire, they remaining subjects of Ahasuerus, fearing the nations; as stated in Megillah (7a): they sent to Esther: "You will arouse jealousy against us among the nations," she responding: "I am already recorded in the chronicles"; wherefore they were compelled to frame the narrative as though praising the might of Ahasuerus; and although this might appear unrelated to th…” In Machshavot Charutz 20:19 (sharing the proof-text Yoma 9b), Rav Tzadok develops the complementary dimension of this principle, illuminating how Yoma 9b anchors the inner service of the heart in Sefer HaZikhronot.

english_source_translation: Bava Kamma 50a: “in the case where one dug the pit on his own property and then renounced ownership of the surrounding area. Consequently, the entire area except for the pit is now open to public passage. In this case, Rabbi Akiva maintains that one who digs a pit on his own property is also liable, not only when the pit is located in the public domain, as it is written: “The owner of the pit shall pay” (Exodus 21:34). Clearly, the Merciful One is referring to a pit that has an owner. Therefore, the owner of the pit pays even if it is located on private property. And Rabbi Yishmael maintains that “the owner of the pit” means that the one responsible for the hazard is liable even if he dug the pit in the public domain and then renounced ownership of it.…”
kisvei_rav_tzadok_parallel: Kisvei Rav Tzadok Parallel — Machshavot Charutz 20:15: “And therefore the leaders initially thought to establish Purim as a full Yom Tov as well; assuming they had already succeeded in blotting out the remembrance of Amalek from the world completely; and there is no greater festival than this.…” In Machshavot Charutz 20:15 (sharing the proof-text Yoma 9b), Rav Tzadok develops the complementary dimension of this principle, illuminating how Bava Kamma 50a anchors the inner service of the heart in Sefer HaZikhronot.
kisvei_ishbitz_radzin_parallel: Kisvei Beis Ishbitz–Radzin Parallel — Beit Yaakov on Torah, Noach 16:4: “as in Bava Kama (50a): “Whoever says the Holy One is indulgent, his innards shall be yielded.”” This teaching from the Ishbitz–Radzin school in Beit Yaakov on Torah, Noach 16:4 (expounding Bava Kamma 50a) supplies the foundational Chassidic lens through which Rav Tzadok frames Bava Kamma 50a in Sefer HaZikhronot.

english_source_translation: Deuteronomy 7: “When the ETERNAL your God brings you to the land that you are about to enter and possess, and dislodges many nations before you—the Hittites, Girgashites, Amorites, Canaanites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites, seven nations much larger than you— and the ETERNAL your God delivers them to you and you defeat them, you must doom them to destruction: grant them no terms and give them no quarter. You shall not intermarry with them: do not give your daughters to their sons or take their daughters for your sons. For they will turn your children away from Me to worship other gods, and GOD’s anger will blaze forth against you, promptly wiping you out.…”
kisvei_rav_tzadok_parallel: Kisvei Rav Tzadok Parallel — Peri Tzadik, Eikev 3:2: “Afterwards Scripture states: 'For you are a holy people unto the Lord your God' (Deuteronomy 7:6), and then: 'Know therefore that the Lord your God, He is God, the faithful God' (Deuteronomy 7:9)—teaching that not only when Israel stands on a lofty rung do they merit perception of Divinity, but even in lowliness they remain bound to the faithful God Who keeps His covenant for a thousand generations.” In Peri Tzadik, Eikev 3:2 (sharing the proof-text Deuteronomy 7:9), Rav Tzadok develops the complementary dimension of this principle, illuminating how Deuteronomy 7 anchors the inner service of the heart in Sefer HaZikhronot.
kisvei_ishbitz_radzin_parallel: Kisvei Beis Ishbitz–Radzin Parallel — Beit Yaakov on Torah, Bereshit 1:1: “In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth: the purpose of all creation is that human beings clarify through free choice that there is no independent power in nature outside the Blessed Creator.” This foundational Ishbitz–Radzin teaching in Beit Yaakov on Torah, Bereshit 1:1 illuminates the Izhbitz-Radzin principle that all natural phenomena are garments for Divine Will underlying Rav Tzadok's thought.

english_source_translation: Berakhot 28b: “After mentioning until when the additional prayer may be recited, the Gemara relates: Rav Avya was ill and did not come to Rav Yosef’s Shabbat lecture. When Rav Avya came the following day, Abaye sought to placate Rav Yosef, and through a series of questions and answers sought to make clear to him that Rav Avya’s failure to attend the lecture was not a display of contempt for Rav Yosef. To this end, he asked him: Why did the Master not attend the Shabbat lecture? Rav Avya said to him: Because my heart was faint and I was unable to attend. Abaye said to him: Why did you not eat something and come? Rav Avya said to him: Does the Master not hold in accordance with that statement of Rav Huna? As Rav Huna said: A person may not taste anything before he recites the additional prayer.…”
kisvei_rav_tzadok_parallel: Kisvei Rav Tzadok Parallel — Divrei Soferim 38:12: “And this is Purim, for the lot (pur) of Haman was transformed into our lot, obligating us to drink, parallel to the first banquet of Ahasuerus where the cure was seeded through Ahasuerus' drunkenness, resulting in Vashti's execution, culminating in Esther's wine banquet; Haman boasting "yea, Esther the queen let no man come in but myself," rejoicing without knowing it was at the cost of his life, drinking the cup of poison rather than gladness; while Esther, who drank with th…” In Divrei Soferim 38:12 (sharing the proof-text Berakhot 28b), Rav Tzadok develops the complementary dimension of this principle, illuminating how Berakhot 28b anchors the inner service of the heart in Sefer HaZikhronot.
kisvei_ishbitz_radzin_parallel: Kisvei Beis Ishbitz–Radzin Parallel — Beit Yaakov on Torah, Bereshit 2:52: “rashly thrusting oneself into every murky concealment and relying antinomian-style on the premise that “His glory fills the earth, so whatever man wishes he may do”—then, heaven forbid, this borders on “another god” (El Acher).” This teaching from the Ishbitz–Radzin school in Beit Yaakov on Torah, Bereshit 2:52 (expounding Isaiah 6:3) supplies the foundational Chassidic lens through which Rav Tzadok frames Berakhot 28b in Sefer HaZikhronot.

english_source_translation: Sefer Yereim: “The 248 positive commands that a person does do not bring one to do evil to creatures or to the Creator, happy is the one who observes them and maintains them. Such a person leaves the world in purity and clean deeds, corresponding to coming to this world in purity. About such a person the verse "blessed are you in your coming and blessed are you in your going" (Deuteronomy 28:6) is said, that your exit from this world should be without sin, just as your coming to this world. And baruch (blessed) has the same gematria as hachi havey (thus you shall exist)”
kisvei_rav_tzadok_parallel: Kisvei Rav Tzadok Parallel — Takanat HaShavin 5:1: “Even when a person stumbles, the inner point of Israel's covenantal bond with Hashem remains untouched in the depths of the heart, and through teshuvah out of love even prior deficiencies are transformed into deeper recognition of His unity.” This parallel in Takanat HaShavin 5:1 directly reinforces Rav Tzadok's exposition here regarding the indestructible root of faith in the heart of Israel.
kisvei_ishbitz_radzin_parallel: Kisvei Beis Ishbitz–Radzin Parallel — Sod Yesharim, Shemini Atzeret 17:2: “The Holy One, blessed be He, looked into the Torah and created the world, clothing the words of Torah within the garments of creation so that Israel would uncover His unity within every detail of life.” This foundational Ishbitz–Radzin teaching in Sod Yesharim, Shemini Atzeret 17:2 illuminates uncovering the inner light of Torah within the garments of creation underlying Rav Tzadok's thought.

english_source_translation: Sanhedrin 90a: “The dispute is with regard to a prophet who prophesies to abolish the essence of the prohibition of idol worship, or a prophet who espouses fulfillment of part of the prohibition and nullification of part of the prohibition of idol worship, asserting that idol worship is permitted in certain circumstances, as the Merciful One says: “And that prophet…shall be put to death; because he has spoken perversion against the Lord…to divert you from the way on which the Lord your God commanded you to walk” (Deuteronomy 13:6). It may be inferred from this verse: If he diverts you even from part of the way. In these cases, Rabbi Shimon holds that he is executed by strangulation, and the Rabbis hold that he is executed by stoning.…”
kisvei_rav_tzadok_parallel_ref: Likkutei Maamarim, Upon Completion of Talmud 5
kisvei_rav_tzadok_parallel: Kisvei Rav Tzadok Parallel — Likkutei Maamarim, Upon Completion of Talmud 5: “And it is known that Nefesh, Ruach, and Neshamah correspond to brain, heart, and liver. And we recite: “The soul You gave within me is pure” (Berakhot 60b), which implies even in the present moment; and that is because the inception of evil is in the heart, as written in chapter HaRoeh (ibid. 61a): that the evil inclination sits upon the portals of the heart.…” In Likkutei Maamarim, Upon Completion of Talmud 5 (sharing the proof-text Sanhedrin 90a, Avodah Zarah 17a), Rav Tzadok develops the complementary dimension of this principle, illuminating how Sanhedrin 90a anchors the inner service of the heart in Sefer HaZikhronot.
kisvei_ishbitz_radzin_parallel: Kisvei Beis Ishbitz–Radzin Parallel — Beit Yaakov on Torah, Noach 45:10: “and likewise what they stated (Sanhedrin 90a): “One who pronounces the Ineffable Name according to its letters has no share in the World to Come.”” This teaching from the Ishbitz–Radzin school in Beit Yaakov on Torah, Noach 45:10 (expounding Sanhedrin 90a) supplies the foundational Chassidic lens through which Rav Tzadok frames Sanhedrin 90a in Sefer HaZikhronot.

english_source_translation: Sanhedrin 100b: “You must say that the attribute of reward is greater than the attribute of punishment, as with regard to the attribute of reward it is written: “He commanded the clouds from above, and opened the doors of heaven, and rained upon them manna to eat” (Psalms 78:23–24). And with regard to the attribute of punishment at the time of the flood the verse says: “And the windows of the heavens were opened” (Genesis 7:11). To mete out punishment, God opened only windows, which are considerably smaller openings than doors, indicating that the attribute of reward is greater.…”
kisvei_rav_tzadok_parallel: Kisvei Rav Tzadok Parallel — Takanat HaShavin 15:71: “And superficially, even without this, what they stated—that "their soul is burned"—is further difficult from the concluding clause of that very Baraisa: according to what I wrote above, that even regarding heretics and their companions whereof they stated "they are not consumed," they are not annihilated completely because the fire of Gehinnom has no dominion to consume them.…” In Takanat HaShavin 15:71 (sharing the proof-text Sanhedrin 100b), Rav Tzadok develops the complementary dimension of this principle, illuminating how Sanhedrin 100b anchors the inner service of the heart in Sefer HaZikhronot.

english_source_translation: Avodah Zarah 17a: “'Remove your way far from her, and come not nigh the door of her house' (Proverbs 5:8): 'Remove your way far from her' refers to heresy (minut); 'and come not nigh the door of her house' refers to the ruling power (or immorality)... Tosafot explains that one must distance oneself as far as possible from the doorway of idolatry and heresy.”
kisvei_rav_tzadok_parallel: Kisvei Rav Tzadok Parallel — Dover Tzedek, Miscellany 4:52: “And these insights are not attained through external intellect—designated in the Gemara in chapter Chelek (Sanhedrin 106b) as "from the lips outward"—but through an absolute acquisition within the heart, which is possible only for one who has tasted and merited to taste of this light.…” In Dover Tzedek, Miscellany 4:52 (sharing the proof-text Avodah Zarah 17a), Rav Tzadok develops the complementary dimension of this principle, illuminating how Avodah Zarah 17a anchors the inner service of the heart in Sefer HaZikhronot.

english_source_translation: Pirkei Avot 3: “Akabyah ben Mahalalel said: mark well three things and you will not come into the power of sin: know from where you come, and where you are going, and before whom you are destined to give an account and reckoning. From where do you come? From a putrid drop. Where are you going? To a place of dust, of worm and of maggot. Before whom you are destined to give an account and reckoning? Before the King of the kings of kings, the Holy One, blessed be He. Rabbi Hanina, the vice-high priest said: pray for the welfare of the government, for were it not for the fear it inspires, every man would swallow his neighbor alive. R.…”
kisvei_rav_tzadok_parallel: Kisvei Rav Tzadok Parallel — Kometz HaMinchah 2:69:1: “Genesis 27:46 “I am weary of my life because of the daughters of Heth”, and in Bereishit Rabbah there 67:12: she cleanses her nose and casts away, meaning: repulsion from their foul spiritual odor, as written concerning Jacob: “See, the smell of my son is as the smell of a field which Hashem has blessed”, and they stated in Berakhot 43b: what is that which the soul derives pleasure from? It is the fragrance; and therefore it is sensed in the nose, for there is the dwelling of…” In Kometz HaMinchah 2:69:1 (sharing the proof-text Proverbs 5:8), Rav Tzadok develops the complementary dimension of this principle, illuminating how Pirkei Avot 3 anchors the inner service of the heart in Sefer HaZikhronot.

kisvei_ishbitz_radzin_parallel: Kisvei Beis Ishbitz–Radzin Parallel — Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 42:4: “And that is: from Creation until Avraham our Father arrived in the world, it appeared to creatures that man was permitted to expand in the bounty bestowed upon him, and say: “My power and the might of mine hand has gotten me this wealth”.…” This teaching from the Ishbitz–Radzin school in Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 42:4 (expounding Deuteronomy 8:17) supplies the foundational Chassidic lens through which Rav Tzadok frames Pirkei Avot 3 in Sefer HaZikhronot.

english_source_translation: Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 1:1 (Rema): “'I have set the Lord always before me' (Psalms 16:8): this is a great principle in the Torah and among the virtues of the righteous who walk before God. For a person's sitting, movements, and dealings while alone in his house are not like his sitting, movements, and dealings when in the presence of a great king; all the more so when a person places in his heart that the Great King, the Holy One, blessed be He, Whose glory fills the whole earth, stands over him and sees his deeds, fear and humility in dread of God will immediately reach him (Guide for the Perplexed III:52).”
kisvei_rav_tzadok_parallel: Kisvei Rav Tzadok Parallel — Sichat Malakhei HaSharet, From Tanchuma 14: “And a wondrous thing: Aristotle, the head of the gentile philosophers in external sciences—which are flawed on their own, serving merely as perfumers and cooks to genuine divine Wisdom—lived likewise in the era of Shimon the Righteous as is known, who was the head of the sages of truth, the masters of the Mishnah and Oral Torah; for "God has made the one corresponding to the other" [Ecclesiastes 7:14].…” In Sichat Malakhei HaSharet, From Tanchuma 14, Rav Tzadok develops the complementary dimension of this principle, illuminating how Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 1:1 anchors the inner service of the heart in Sefer HaZikhronot.

kisvei_ishbitz_radzin_parallel: Kisvei Beis Ishbitz–Radzin Parallel — Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Lech Lecha 1: “'Go for yourself from your land, from your birthplace, and from your father's house' (Genesis 12:1): a person must continually strip away habitual assumptions and natural reliances so as to walk solely by the living illumination of God's word in the present moment.” This foundational Ishbitz–Radzin teaching in Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Lech Lecha 1 illuminates the Mei HaShiloach's teaching on transcending habitual nature through living faith underlying Rav Tzadok's thought.

To mete out punishment, God opened only windows, which are considerably smaller openings than doors, indicating that the attribute of reward is greater.…”
kisvei_rav_tzadok_parallel: Kisvei Rav Tzadok Parallel — Divrei Chalomot 27:1: “Friday night of the holy Shabbat of Parashat Behar, the year Birchoteha [5632 / 1872]: Concerning why the curses and imprecations of Mount Ebal are explicitly articulated in the Written Torah, whereas the blessings of Mount Gerizim are not detailed: For that which is stated in the Written Torah—which is transcribed and laid open to all—consists of matters that are overt, perceptible to all, and visible to the eye; but that which is not perceptible to the physical eye was tran…” In Divrei Chalomot 27:1 (sharing the proof-text Sanhedrin 90a), Rav Tzadok develops the complementary dimension of this principle, illuminating how Sanhedrin 100b anchors the inner service of the heart in Sefer HaZikhronot.
kisvei_ishbitz_radzin_parallel: Kisvei Beis Ishbitz–Radzin Parallel — Beit Yaakov on Torah, Noach 45:10: “and likewise what they stated (Sanhedrin 90a): “One who pronounces the Ineffable Name according to its letters has no share in the World to Come.”” This teaching from the Ishbitz–Radzin school in Beit Yaakov on Torah, Noach 45:10 (expounding Sanhedrin 90a) supplies the foundational Chassidic lens through which Rav Tzadok frames Sanhedrin 100b in Sefer HaZikhronot.

english_source_translation: Chullin 10a: “It is due to the fact that it is the typical manner of creeping animals to expose the contents of a vessel so that they may drink. Therefore, the exposure of the water is attributed to a creeping animal or to a ritually pure person. By contrast, in a case where he left the vessel exposed and found it covered, the concern is that it was an impure man who covered it, since it is not the typical manner of creeping animals to cover exposed vessels. Evidently, with regard to prohibition or ritual impurity, there are circumstances of uncertainty when the ruling is lenient.…”
kisvei_rav_tzadok_parallel: Kisvei Rav Tzadok Parallel — Kometz HaMinchah 2:69:1: “Genesis 27:46 “I am weary of my life because of the daughters of Heth”, and in Bereishit Rabbah there 67:12: she cleanses her nose and casts away, meaning: repulsion from their foul spiritual odor, as written concerning Jacob: “See, the smell of my son is as the smell of a field which Hashem has blessed”, and they stated in Berakhot 43b: what is that which the soul derives pleasure from? It is the fragrance; and therefore it is sensed in the nose, for there is the dwelling of…” In Kometz HaMinchah 2:69:1 (sharing the proof-text Proverbs 5:8), Rav Tzadok develops the complementary dimension of this principle, illuminating how Chullin 10a anchors the inner service of the heart in Sefer HaZikhronot.
kisvei_ishbitz_radzin_parallel_ref: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 42:4
kisvei_ishbitz_radzin_parallel: Kisvei Beis Ishbitz–Radzin Parallel — Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 42:4: “And that is: from Creation until Avraham our Father arrived in the world, it appeared to creatures that man was permitted to expand in the bounty bestowed upon him, and say: “My power and the might of mine hand has gotten me this wealth”.…” This teaching from the Ishbitz–Radzin school in Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 42:4 (expounding Deuteronomy 8:17) supplies the foundational Chassidic lens through which Rav Tzadok frames Chullin 10a in Sefer HaZikhronot.

english_source_translation: Menachot 99b: “the apparent dereliction of the study of Torah is its foundation, e.g., if one breaks off his studies in order to participate in a funeral or a wedding procession. This is derived from a verse, as it is written: “And the Lord said to Moses: Hew for yourself two tablets of stone like the first, and I will write upon the tablets the words that were on the first tablets, which [asher] you broke” (Exodus 34:1). The word “asher” is an allusion to the fact that that the Holy One, Blessed be He, said to Moses: Your strength is true [yishar koḥakha] in that you broke the tablets, as the breaking of the first tablets led to the foundation of the Torah through the giving of the second tablets.…”
kisvei_rav_tzadok_parallel: Kisvei Rav Tzadok Parallel — Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Ner HaMitzvot 2:38: “In this same manner regarding the spiritual "Woman" (the receptive study of Torah), it is taught in Menachot (99b): the verse "it shall not depart from your mouth" was stated as a blessing; but as an obligatory commandment, it is fulfilled by studying once in the morning [the attribute of day, masculine] and once in the evening [the attribute of night, feminine], which correspond to male and female.…” In Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Ner HaMitzvot 2:38 (sharing the proof-text Menachot 99b), Rav Tzadok develops the complementary dimension of this principle, illuminating how Menachot 99b anchors the inner service of the heart in Sefer HaZikhronot.
kisvei_ishbitz_radzin_parallel_ref: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Lech Lecha 1
kisvei_ishbitz_radzin_parallel: Kisvei Beis Ishbitz–Radzin Parallel — Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Lech Lecha 1: “'Go for yourself from your land, from your birthplace, and from your father's house' (Genesis 12:1): a person must continually strip away habitual assumptions and natural reliances so as to walk solely by the living illumination of God's word in the present moment.” This foundational Ishbitz–Radzin teaching in Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Lech Lecha 1 illuminates the Mei HaShiloach's teaching on transcending habitual nature through living faith underlying Rav Tzadok's thought.

english_source_translation: Berakhot 12b: “With regard to bowing, the Gemara relates: When Rav Sheshet bowed he bowed all at once, like a cane, without delay. When he stood upright he stood upright like a snake, lifting himself slowly, demonstrating that the awe of God was upon him in the manner that he bowed and stood upright (HaBoneh). And, with regard to the formulation of the blessings, Rabba bar Ḥinnana Sava said in the name of Rav: Throughout the year a person prays and concludes the third blessing of the Amida prayer with: The holy God, and concludes the blessing regarding the restoration of justice to Israel with: King who loves righteousness and justice, with the exception of the ten days between Rosh HaShana and Yom Kippur, the Ten Days of Atonement.…”
kisvei_rav_tzadok_parallel: Kisvei Rav Tzadok Parallel — Dover Tzedek, Miscellany 4:12: “And it is taught in Bava Batra (14b): Moses wrote his book and the section of Balaam. The meaning: "his book" represents the inscription of the divine Wisdom (Chochmah) seated in Moses' mind, the Zohar equating "book" with Chochmah. Whereas the section of Balaam lay outside Moses' regular conduit of Wisdom, Moses being its holy antithesis, buried opposite Beit Peor. And he could not directly channel that degraded wisdom hidden away in accidental, casual happenings.…” In Dover Tzedek, Miscellany 4:12 (sharing the proof-text Berakhot 12b), Rav Tzadok develops the complementary dimension of this principle, illuminating how Berakhot 12b anchors the inner service of the heart in Sefer HaZikhronot.
kisvei_ishbitz_radzin_parallel_ref: Sod Yesharim, The Seventh Night of Pesach 14:1
kisvei_ishbitz_radzin_parallel: Kisvei Beis Ishbitz–Radzin Parallel — Sod Yesharim, The Seventh Night of Pesach 14:1: “At the Splitting of the Sea, Israel merited to see how all the circuitous paths of exile and the terrifying pursuit of Egypt were orchestrated solely to reveal the sovereignty of Heaven, fulfilling the obligation to remember the Exodus both by day (in times of clarity) and by night (in times of darkness).” This teaching from the Ishbitz–Radzin school in Sod Yesharim, The Seventh Night of Pesach 14:1 (expounding Berakhot 12b) supplies the foundational Chassidic lens through which Rav Tzadok frames Berakhot 12b in Sefer HaZikhronot.

english_source_translation: Yalkut Shimoni, Eikev §851 (and Berakhot 35b): “Wherever Scripture mentions eating and satiation, you find an admonition against forgetting God ('And you shall eat and be satisfied—take heed to yourselves lest your heart be deceived'; 'When you have eaten and are satisfied... beware lest you forget the Lord your God'). And in Berakhot 35b: Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa said: Whoever derives benefit from this world without a blessing is as though he robs the Holy One, blessed be He, and the Congregation of Israel.”
kisvei_rav_tzadok_parallel: Kisvei Rav Tzadok Parallel — Divrei Soferim 11:1: “Through eating and drinking a person arrives at haughtiness, as written in Berakhot [10b]: "Only after this one has exalted himself in pride...", and it seems to me that this applies specifically to eating and drinking prior to prayer, where one imagines he possesses the independent power to sustain his life, which is the height of pride; and furthermore, through food and drink a person attains settled clarity, as stated in Bava Batra [12b]: "Before one has eaten and drunk he…” In Divrei Soferim 11:1 (sharing the proof-text Berakhot 10b), Rav Tzadok develops the complementary dimension of this principle, illuminating how Yalkut Shimoni on Torah 851 anchors the inner service of the heart in Sefer HaZikhronot.
kisvei_ishbitz_radzin_parallel_ref: Sod Yesharim, The Seventh Day of Pesach 23:2
kisvei_ishbitz_radzin_parallel: Kisvei Beis Ishbitz–Radzin Parallel — Sod Yesharim, The Seventh Day of Pesach 23:2: “'And the Lord showed him a tree, and he cast it into the waters, and the waters were made sweet' (Exodus 15:25): the tree of the Torah sweetens the bitter waters of worldly anxiety, teaching that through prayer and faith even a decree that has already been sealed can be transformed into mercy.” This teaching from the Ishbitz–Radzin school in Sod Yesharim, The Seventh Day of Pesach 23:2 (expounding Berakhot 10b) supplies the foundational Chassidic lens through which Rav Tzadok frames Yalkut Shimoni on Torah 851 in Sefer HaZikhronot.

english_source_translation: Berakhot 10b: “Similarly, Rabbi Ḥanan said: Even if the master of dreams, in a true dream, an angel (Ma’ayan HaBerakhot) tells a person that tomorrow he will die, he should not prevent himself from praying for mercy, as it is stated: “For in the multitude of dreams and vanities there are many words; but fear God” (Ecclesiastes 5:6). Although the dream may seem real to him, that is not necessarily the case, and one must place his trust in God. Having heard Isaiah’s harsh prophecy, immediately “Hezekiah turned his face toward the wall and prayed to the Lord” (Isaiah 38:2).…”
kisvei_rav_tzadok_parallel: Kisvei Rav Tzadok Parallel — Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Ner HaMitzvot 2:65: “And the zav (flux) embodies physical lust, which is generally pleasing to creatures, and he remains within human society as well as within the general camp of Israel who are vulnerable to this temptation, as stated in Sanhedrin (63b): "Israel served idols only to permit public sexual immorality"; and at the end of chapter Chavit (Shabbat 147b): the wine of Perugita and water of Diyoamsit caused the exile of the Ten Tribes, matching: "Jeshurun grew fat and kicked.…” In Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Ner HaMitzvot 2:65 (sharing the proof-text Berakhot 10b), Rav Tzadok develops the complementary dimension of this principle, illuminating how Berakhot 10b anchors the inner service of the heart in Sefer HaZikhronot.
kisvei_ishbitz_radzin_parallel_ref: Sod Yesharim, The Seventh Day of Pesach 23:2
kisvei_ishbitz_radzin_parallel: Kisvei Beis Ishbitz–Radzin Parallel — Sod Yesharim, The Seventh Day of Pesach 23:2: “'And the Lord showed him a tree, and he cast it into the waters, and the waters were made sweet' (Exodus 15:25): the tree of the Torah sweetens the bitter waters of worldly anxiety, teaching that through prayer and faith even a decree that has already been sealed can be transformed into mercy.” This teaching from the Ishbitz–Radzin school in Sod Yesharim, The Seventh Day of Pesach 23:2 (expounding Berakhot 10b) supplies the foundational Chassidic lens through which Rav Tzadok frames Berakhot 10b in Sefer HaZikhronot.

english_source_translation: Berakhot 21a: “The Gemara challenges: And prayer, which is also a matter in which the community is engaged, and we learned in the mishna: One who was standing in prayer and remembered that he is one who experienced a seminal emission and did not yet immerse himself should not interrupt his prayer, rather he should abridge it. The Gemara infers: The reason is because he already began to pray; however, if he did not yet begin, then he should not begin, even by means of contemplation. The Gemara responds: Prayer is different in that it does not contain the acceptance of the yoke of the kingdom of Heaven.…”
kisvei_rav_tzadok_parallel: Kisvei Rav Tzadok Parallel — Dover Tzedek, Miscellany 4:89: “And it is known that the returning echo resembles the voice of the speaker [yet modifies according to the receiving vessel, hence manifesting in a different tongue]; and the returning echo of Torah is that the Holy One recites the teaching opposite him, which occurs uniquely at night, expounded from "in the night His song shall be with me".…” In Dover Tzedek, Miscellany 4:89 (sharing the proof-text Berakhot 21a), Rav Tzadok develops the complementary dimension of this principle, illuminating how Berakhot 21a anchors the inner service of the heart in Sefer HaZikhronot.
kisvei_ishbitz_radzin_parallel: Kisvei Beis Ishbitz–Radzin Parallel — Sod Yesharim, Shemini Atzeret 17:2: “The Holy One, blessed be He, looked into the Torah and created the world, clothing the words of Torah within the garments of creation so that Israel would uncover His unity within every detail of life.” This foundational Ishbitz–Radzin teaching in Sod Yesharim, Shemini Atzeret 17:2 illuminates uncovering the inner light of Torah within the garments of creation underlying Rav Tzadok's thought.

english_source_translation: Shabbat 149a: “GEMARA: We learned in the mishna that one may not read the names of his guests or the appetizers served in his meal from a written list. The Gemara asks: What is the reason for this prohibition? Rav Beivai said: It is a decree lest one erase something that is written on the list if he regrets inviting a particular guest or changes his mind about a particular dish. Abaye said: It is a decree lest one read regular business documents. The Gemara asks: What is the practical difference between them? The Gemara answers: There is a difference between them in a case in which the writing is on a wall and it is raised higher than a person can reach.…”
kisvei_rav_tzadok_parallel: Kisvei Rav Tzadok Parallel — Peri Tzadik, Mishpatim 4:1: “'I shall sing in praises to enter within the openings of the apple orchard' (Azamer be-Shvachin): this corresponds to 'Open for me the gates of righteousness' (Psalms 118:19), entering the Garden of Eden where the Shekhinah dwells among Israel and purifies the camp from every blemish.” In Peri Tzadik, Mishpatim 4:1 (sharing the proof-text Shabbat 149a), Rav Tzadok develops the complementary dimension of this principle, illuminating how Shabbat 149a anchors the inner service of the heart in Sefer HaZikhronot.
kisvei_ishbitz_radzin_parallel: Kisvei Beis Ishbitz–Radzin Parallel — Beit Yaakov on Torah, Noach 52:84: “Fulfilling Habakkuk 2:4, 'The righteous shall live by his faith': true life consists of recognizing that all human strength and wisdom flow moment by moment from the Creator alone.” This foundational Ishbitz–Radzin teaching in Beit Yaakov on Torah, Noach 52:84 illuminates living by emunah as the single foundation of all the commandments underlying Rav Tzadok's thought.

english_source_translation: Rashi on Shabbat 149a: “Primary source background in Rashi on Shabbat 149a illuminating Rav Tzadok's teaching in this passage.”
kisvei_rav_tzadok_parallel: Kisvei Rav Tzadok Parallel — Peri Tzadik, Mishpatim 4:1: “'I shall sing in praises to enter within the openings of the apple orchard' (Azamer be-Shvachin): this corresponds to 'Open for me the gates of righteousness' (Psalms 118:19), entering the Garden of Eden where the Shekhinah dwells among Israel and purifies the camp from every blemish.” In Peri Tzadik, Mishpatim 4:1 (sharing the proof-text Shabbat 149a), Rav Tzadok develops the complementary dimension of this principle, illuminating how Rashi on Shabbat 149a anchors the inner service of the heart in Sefer HaZikhronot.
kisvei_ishbitz_radzin_parallel: Kisvei Beis Ishbitz–Radzin Parallel — Sod Yesharim, Shemini Atzeret 17:2: “The Holy One, blessed be He, looked into the Torah and created the world, clothing the words of Torah within the garments of creation so that Israel would uncover His unity within every detail of life.” This foundational Ishbitz–Radzin teaching in Sod Yesharim, Shemini Atzeret 17:2 illuminates uncovering the inner light of Torah within the garments of creation underlying Rav Tzadok's thought.

english_source_translation: Berakhot 32b: “Rabbi Elazar said: This story proves that prayer is greater than good deeds without prayer (Tosafot), as there was none greater in the performance of good deeds than Moses our teacher; nevertheless, his request was granted, albeit in a limited manner, in his request to enter Eretz Yisrael, only through prayer, when God permitted him to climb the mountain and look out over the land. As, initially it is stated: “Speak no more to Me,” juxtaposed to which is: “Go up to the summit of the mountain.” After comparing and contrasting prayer and good deeds, the Gemara explores another comparison. Rabbi Elazar said: A fast is greater than charity.…”
kisvei_rav_tzadok_parallel: Kisvei Rav Tzadok Parallel — Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Ner HaMitzvot 2:110: “One may explain this according to both views: as recorded in Berakhot (32b) regarding the Pious Men of Old (Chasidim HaRishonim), who would spend nine hours each day preparing and praying to direct their hearts to the Omnipresent; which is the "service of the heart" (Ta'anit 2a), embodying Reverent Awe as we wrote above. Therefore Rabban Gamliel said (Berakhot 34b) that a servant before the king can accomplish more through prayer, for this belongs to his specific domain.…” In Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Ner HaMitzvot 2:110 (sharing the proof-text Berakhot 32b), Rav Tzadok develops the complementary dimension of this principle, illuminating how Berakhot 32b anchors the inner service of the heart in Sefer HaZikhronot.
kisvei_ishbitz_radzin_parallel: Kisvei Beis Ishbitz–Radzin Parallel — Sod Yesharim, Parashat Shekalim 2:2: “At the beginning of the month of Adar, the Holy One, blessed be He, begins to arrange the supernal order of direct illumination (or yashar) for the coming year; therefore Israel gives the half-shekel to uproot thekelipah of Amalek (doubt and chance) and anchor their hearts in Divine providence.” This teaching from the Ishbitz–Radzin school in Sod Yesharim, Parashat Shekalim 2:2 (expounding Berakhot 32b) supplies the foundational Chassidic lens through which Rav Tzadok frames Berakhot 32b in Sefer HaZikhronot.

english_source_translation: Jerusalem Talmud Chagigah 1:7: “MISHNAH: Rebbi Simeon ben Menassiah says, who is distorted cannot be repaired? This is one committing incest or adultery and producing a bastard. If you would say a thief or robber, that one may repent and repair. Rebbi Simeon ben Menassia says, one calls distorted only what was correct before and became distorted. Who is that? This is a scholar who separated from the Torah. HALAKHAH: Rebbi Simeon ben Yoḥai stated: When you see towns in the Land of Israel uprooted from their place, know that they did not contribute to the wages of Bible and Mishnah teachers(2).. What is the reason? Why is the land ruined, torn down like an uninhabited wilderness? The Eternal said, because they abandoned My Torah. 9:11-12..…”
kisvei_rav_tzadok_parallel: Kisvei Rav Tzadok Parallel — Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Ner HaMitzvot 2:258: “And regarding this they said in Berakhot (32b): "From the day the Temple was destroyed, an iron wall intervened between Israel and their Father in heaven." The meaning: a wall exists only in physical deed; since the Temple fell, our capacity for action deteriorated, most practical mitzvot being lost and the remainder performed feebly due to the oppression of kingdoms. As stated in Berakhot (17a): "It is our will to perform Your will...…” In Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Ner HaMitzvot 2:258 (sharing the proof-text Berakhot 32b), Rav Tzadok develops the complementary dimension of this principle, illuminating how Jerusalem Talmud Chagigah 1:7 anchors the inner service of the heart in Sefer HaZikhronot.
kisvei_ishbitz_radzin_parallel: Kisvei Beis Ishbitz–Radzin Parallel — Sod Yesharim, Parashat Shekalim 2:2: “At the beginning of the month of Adar, the Holy One, blessed be He, begins to arrange the supernal order of direct illumination (or yashar) for the coming year; therefore Israel gives the half-shekel to uproot thekelipah of Amalek (doubt and chance) and anchor their hearts in Divine providence.” This teaching from the Ishbitz–Radzin school in Sod Yesharim, Parashat Shekalim 2:2 (expounding Berakhot 32b) supplies the foundational Chassidic lens through which Rav Tzadok frames Jerusalem Talmud Chagigah 1:7 in Sefer HaZikhronot.

english_source_translation: Kiddushin 30b: ““Say to wisdom: You are my sister, and call understanding your kinswoman” (Proverbs 7:4), which indicates that one should be as knowledgeable in the Torah as in the identity of his sister. And it states: “Bind them upon your fingers, you shall write them upon the tablet of your heart” (Proverbs 7:3). And it states: “As arrows in the hand of a mighty man, so are the children of one’s youth” (Psalms 127:4). And it states: “Sharp arrows of the mighty” (Psalms 120:4). And it states: “Your arrows are sharp, the peoples fall under you” (Psalms 45:6). And it states: “Happy is the man who has his quiver full of them; they shall not be put to shame when they speak with their enemies in the gate” (Psalms 127:5).…”
kisvei_rav_tzadok_parallel: Kisvei Rav Tzadok Parallel — Dover Tzedek, Miscellany 4:119: “And behold, it returns through the Oral Torah which ascended in our hands from Babylonia, as I wrote elsewhere: just as the Written Torah was forged in the Egyptian exile, where they refined and elevated the Giving of the Written Torah, so the Oral Torah was shaped in the Babylonian exile, ascending thence with them through the Sages of the Mishnah, headed by the Men of the Great Assembly (Avot 1:1), who formulated: "Raise up many disciples" and "Make a fence around the Torah…” In Dover Tzedek, Miscellany 4:119 (sharing the proof-text Daniel 1:4), Rav Tzadok develops the complementary dimension of this principle, illuminating how Kiddushin 30b anchors the inner service of the heart in Sefer HaZikhronot.
kisvei_ishbitz_radzin_parallel: Kisvei Beis Ishbitz–Radzin Parallel — Beit Yaakov on Torah, Noach 54:13: “And this explains Yoma (9b): “Regarding the Second Temple, whose sin was not openly manifest, their end of exile was not revealed; and why were they exiled? Because of baseless hatred (sin'at chinam).”” This teaching from the Ishbitz–Radzin school in Beit Yaakov on Torah, Noach 54:13 (expounding Yoma 9b) supplies the foundational Chassidic lens through which Rav Tzadok frames Kiddushin 30b in Sefer HaZikhronot.

english_source_translation: Tosafot on Berakhot 17a: “Concerning the statement 'Whoever performs a mitzvah not for its own sake (shelo lishmah), it were better for him had he never been created,' whereas Rav Yehudah said in the name of Rav, 'A person should always engage in Torah and mitzvot even not for their own sake, for out of doing them not for their own sake he comes to do them for their own sake': Tosafot explains that the condemnation applies only to one who studies solely to vex and contend with his fellows, whereas one who studies for honor or reward is encouraged to continue until he attains pure motivation.”
kisvei_rav_tzadok_parallel: Kisvei Rav Tzadok Parallel — Resisei Layla 6:2: “Likewise, prayer in its essence is rooted in a broken heart, as it is written (Psalms 51:19): "A broken and contrite heart, etc., You will not despise," and they taught (Zohar Part I, 23b): "The prayer of the poor man envelops all prayers.…” In Resisei Layla 6:2 (sharing the proof-text Pesachim 50b), Rav Tzadok develops the complementary dimension of this principle, illuminating how Tosafot on Berakhot 17a anchors the inner service of the heart in Sefer HaZikhronot.
kisvei_ishbitz_radzin_parallel: Kisvei Beis Ishbitz–Radzin Parallel — Tiferet Yosef, Bereshit 1:1: “The Torah opens with 'In the beginning' to teach that even within the darkness and concealment of this world ('and darkness was upon the face of the deep'), a person who seeks Hashem discovers that the darkness itself is a garment concealing His supernal light.” This foundational Ishbitz–Radzin teaching in Tiferet Yosef, Bereshit 1:1 illuminates finding Divine unity within the concealment of the natural order underlying Rav Tzadok's thought.

english_source_translation: Pesachim 50b: “The Sages stated a principle: And a person may not deviate from the local custom, due to potential dispute. Similarly, one who transports Sabbatical Year produce from a place where a crop has ceased in the fields to a place where it has not yet ceased or from a place where it has not yet ceased to a place where it has already ceased is obligated to remove the produce from his possession, in accordance with the stringencies of both locations. It is permitted for homeowners to eat Sabbatical Year produce in their houses only as long as that species of fruit remains in the field as ownerless property. However, once that particular fruit is no longer available for animals in the fields, one is required to remove what remains of that species from his home.…”
kisvei_rav_tzadok_parallel: Kisvei Rav Tzadok Parallel — Resisei Layla 25:1: “Man does not remain constantly in a single order and status, and he constantly experiences spiritual ascents and descents, as is known to all who examine their ways. And this reflects what Hashem, blessed be He, established within Creation concerning the diminution of the moon; for it is known that the sun and moon allude to the Holy One, blessed be He, and His Shechinah, the moon alluding to the Congregation of Israel who receive their light from the sun, "'For a sun and a s…” In Resisei Layla 25:1 (sharing the proof-text Pesachim 50b), Rav Tzadok develops the complementary dimension of this principle, illuminating how Pesachim 50b anchors the inner service of the heart in Sefer HaZikhronot.
kisvei_ishbitz_radzin_parallel: Kisvei Beis Ishbitz–Radzin Parallel — Sod Yesharim, Rosh Hashanah 33:2: “'Recite before Me Zikhronot (Remembrances), so that your remembrance may ascend before Me for good' (Rosh Hashanah 16a): when a person below remembers that every breath and movement stems from the Creator, he awakens supernal remembrance on High.” This foundational Ishbitz–Radzin teaching in Sod Yesharim, Rosh Hashanah 33:2 illuminates the mystical power of zikhronot (remembrance) uniting human awareness with Divine providence underlying Rav Tzadok's thought.

english_source_translation: Kiddushin 39b: “The Gemara asks concerning one whose father told him to ascend a loft and bring young birds (fulfilling both honoring parents and sending away the mother bird) and who fell and died on his return: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that perhaps he was pondering idolatry in his heart, for regarding idolatry even a sinful thought is punished, as it is written: 'That I may take the house of Israel in their own heart' (Ezekiel 14:5).”
kisvei_rav_tzadok_parallel: Kisvei Rav Tzadok Parallel — Takanat HaShavin 2:8: “And therefore the Sages said [in Koheles Rabbah] of the wisdom of Shlomo HaMelech that he knew “how to heal the past” — meaning to remedy the ailments of the soul in the sins that came before; and likewise what they said there, that he knew “how one sweetens the lupine [tormus],” which alludes to transgressions — for “it is evil and bitter, your forsaking Hashem” (Yirmeyah 2:19)] is your forsaking Hashem” as the very definition of sin — a bitterness that Shlomo’s wisdom knew …” In Takanat HaShavin 2:8 (sharing the proof-text Sanhedrin 56b), Rav Tzadok develops the complementary dimension of this principle, illuminating how Kiddushin 39b anchors the inner service of the heart in Sefer HaZikhronot.
kisvei_ishbitz_radzin_parallel: Kisvei Beis Ishbitz–Radzin Parallel — Beit Yaakov on Torah, Bereshit 9:10: “nevertheless, a wholesome person is granted a foretaste of the fruit of his deeds in this world (Kiddushin 40a), because worldly pleasures are meant to support and strengthen his divine service.” This teaching from the Ishbitz–Radzin school in Beit Yaakov on Torah, Bereshit 9:10 (expounding Kiddushin 40a) supplies the foundational Chassidic lens through which Rav Tzadok frames Kiddushin 39b in Sefer HaZikhronot.

english_source_translation: Kiddushin 40a: “soldiers [nosei keisar] who guarded me all night. They said to him: Perhaps a matter of forbidden intercourse presented itself to you and you were saved from it, which is why a miracle occurred for you. As we learned: With regard to anyone to whom a matter of forbidden intercourse presented itself to him and he was saved from it, a miracle is performed for him. As it says: “Mighty in strength who fulfill His word, hearkening to the voice of His word” (Psalms 103:20). This is referring to one such as Rabbi Tzadok and his colleagues. To what is this referring? Rabbi Tzadok was enticed by a certain noblewoman to engage in sexual intercourse with her.…”
kisvei_rav_tzadok_parallel: Kisvei Rav Tzadok Parallel — Takanat HaShavin 2:8: “And therefore the Sages said [in Koheles Rabbah] of the wisdom of Shlomo HaMelech that he knew “how to heal the past” — meaning to remedy the ailments of the soul in the sins that came before; and likewise what they said there, that he knew “how one sweetens the lupine [tormus],” which alludes to transgressions — for “it is evil and bitter, your forsaking Hashem” (Yirmeyah 2:19)] is your forsaking Hashem” as the very definition of sin — a bitterness that Shlomo’s wisdom knew …” In Takanat HaShavin 2:8 (sharing the proof-text Sanhedrin 56b), Rav Tzadok develops the complementary dimension of this principle, illuminating how Kiddushin 40a anchors the inner service of the heart in Sefer HaZikhronot.
kisvei_ishbitz_radzin_parallel: Kisvei Beis Ishbitz–Radzin Parallel — Beit Yaakov on Torah, Bereshit 9:10: “nevertheless, a wholesome person is granted a foretaste of the fruit of his deeds in this world (Kiddushin 40a), because worldly pleasures are meant to support and strengthen his divine service.” This teaching from the Ishbitz–Radzin school in Beit Yaakov on Torah, Bereshit 9:10 (expounding Kiddushin 40a) supplies the foundational Chassidic lens through which Rav Tzadok frames Kiddushin 40a in Sefer HaZikhronot.

english_source_translation: Sanhedrin 56b: “Rabbi Ḥananya ben Gamla says: The descendants of Noah are also commanded concerning the prohibition against consuming the blood from a living animal. Rabbi Shimon says: They are also commanded concerning the prohibition against engaging in sorcery. Rabbi Yosei says: With regard to every type of sorcery that is stated in the passage about sorcery, it is prohibited for a descendant of Noah to engage in it. This is derived from the verses: “When you come into the land that the Lord your God gives you, you shall not learn to do like the abominations of those nations.…”

kisvei_ishbitz_radzin_parallel: Kisvei Beis Ishbitz–Radzin Parallel — Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Lech Lecha 1: “'Go for yourself from your land, from your birthplace, and from your father's house' (Genesis 12:1): a person must continually strip away habitual assumptions and natural reliances so as to walk solely by the living illumination of God's word in the present moment.” This foundational Ishbitz–Radzin teaching in Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Lech Lecha 1 illuminates the Mei HaShiloach's teaching on transcending habitual nature through living faith underlying Rav Tzadok's thought.

english_source_translation: Responsa Chacham Tzvi §18: “Concerning the report that I stated in the study hall that the Blessed Name and nature (ha-teva) are all one: I declare that so I said, and I maintain it! Yet know that the term 'teva' in this sense is an invention of later scholars four or five centuries ago and is not found in the words of our early Sages; rather, it is the Holy One, blessed be He, Who causes the wind to blow, brings down the rain, and causes the dew to descend. Thus what later authors call 'nature' is in truth nothing other than Divine Providence itself.”

kisvei_ishbitz_radzin_parallel: Kisvei Beis Ishbitz–Radzin Parallel — Sod Yesharim, Rosh Hashanah 33:2: “'Recite before Me Zikhronot (Remembrances), so that your remembrance may ascend before Me for good' (Rosh Hashanah 16a): when a person below remembers that every breath and movement stems from the Creator, he awakens supernal remembrance on High.” This foundational Ishbitz–Radzin teaching in Sod Yesharim, Rosh Hashanah 33:2 illuminates the mystical power of zikhronot (remembrance) uniting human awareness with Divine providence underlying Rav Tzadok's thought.

english_source_translation: Moed Katan 28a: “Rava said: Length of life, children, and sustenance depend not upon merit, but upon mazal (astral destiny).”
kisvei_rav_tzadok_parallel: Kisvei Rav Tzadok Parallel — Machshavot Charutz 8:3: “And the Crown of Torah which is exalted above them all is the spiritual rung of Hu [He]; which is the transcendent, concealed depth unto which all the seed of Israel are cleaved; wherefore they all merited receiving the Torah, which He did not do for any gentile nation (Tehillim 147:20), who possess no connection to this concealed root; from which supernal Chochmah is drawn ex nihilo from Ayin, as is known; and the "fallen fruit" (novelot) of this supernal wisdom is the Torah…” In Machshavot Charutz 8:3 (sharing the proof-text Moed Katan 28a), Rav Tzadok develops the complementary dimension of this principle, illuminating how Moed Katan 28a anchors the inner service of the heart in Sefer HaZikhronot.

english_source_translation: Sanhedrin 67b: “one type of death penalty, namely, decapitation. Since that is the only type of capital punishment that applies to gentiles, it cannot be derived through a verbal analogy that the same type applies to a Jewish sorceror. The baraita continues: Ben Azzai says that it is stated: “You shall not allow a witch to live” (Exodus 22:17), and it is stated in the following verse: “Whoever lies with an animal shall be put to death” (Exodus 22:18). The fact that the Torah juxtaposes this matter to that matter is to teach that just as one who lies with an animal is executed by stoning (see Leviticus, chapter 20), so too, a warlock is executed by stoning.…”
kisvei_rav_tzadok_parallel: Kisvei Rav Tzadok Parallel — Resisei Layla 15:1: “There are two forms of divine comprehension: one is general, which is equal across all Israel, inasmuch as they are believers, children of believers, an inheritance from the Patriarchs, that there is a God Who creates, supervises, possesses omnipotence, etc.…” In Resisei Layla 15:1 (sharing the proof-text Sanhedrin 67b, Chullin 7b), Rav Tzadok develops the complementary dimension of this principle, illuminating how Sanhedrin 67b anchors the inner service of the heart in Sefer HaZikhronot.

english_source_translation: Avodah Zarah 54b: “But rather, it is derived from the case of vessels of the Temple that Ahaz used for idol worship, as it is written: “And all the vessels, which King Ahaz in his reign did cast away when he acted treacherously, we have prepared and sanctified, and behold, they are before the altar of the Lord” (II Chronicles 29:19). And the Master said: “We have prepared” means that we interred them; “and sanctified” means that we sanctified other vessels in their stead, as the original vessels were prohibited. But how could Ahaz render the vessels of the Temple forbidden, as a person does not render forbidden an item that is not his? Rather, since Ahaz performed a sacrificial rite upon them in idolatrous worship, the vessels were prohibited.…”

english_source_translation: Chullin 7b: “'There is none else besides Him' (Deuteronomy 4:35): Rabbi Chanina said: Even sorcery has no independent power! When a certain woman sought to take earth from beneath Rabbi Chanina's feet to perform sorcery against him, he said to her: 'Take it, for your sorcery will not succeed: it is written, There is none else besides Him!' Why then did Rabbi Yochanan say that sorcery is called keshafim because it diminishes the heavenly retinue? Rabbi Chanina was different because his merit was exceedingly great.”

english_source_translation: Moed Katan 16b: “so too, the words of Torah, which are “the work of the hands of an artist,” i.e., God, must remain hidden in the study hall. Despite Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi’s decree, Rabbi Ḥiyya went out and taught his two nephews, Rav and Rabba bar bar Ḥana, in the marketplace. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi heard what he had done and became angry with him. When Rabbi Ḥiyya came at some later date to visit him, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi mockingly said to him: Iyya, who is calling you outside? By asking this question Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi was intimating that Rabbi Ḥiyya should leave his house. Rabbi Ḥiyya understood that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi had taken the matter to heart and was insulted, and so he conducted himself as if he had been admonished, as a self-imposed punishment, for thirty days.…”
kisvei_rav_tzadok_parallel_ref: Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 16:29
kisvei_rav_tzadok_parallel: Kisvei Rav Tzadok Parallel — Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 16:29: “And in the episode of Haman which was brought about through the matter of Saul and David in acting contrary to the explicit commandment, concerning which was Haman's prosecutorial claim: that this too appeared outwardly as stiff-neckedness and a failure to be drawn after Hashem, blessed be He, being termed 'wise in your own eyes' (Proverbs 3:7), in that it was drawn from a wisdom of superficial appearance, and not that which is wisdom in ultimate Truth; and this is the entire…” In Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 16:29 (sharing the proof-text Moed Katan 16b, Bava Batra 75b), Rav Tzadok develops the complementary dimension of this principle, illuminating how Moed Katan 16b anchors the inner service of the heart in Sefer HaZikhronot.

english_source_translation: Bava Batra 75b: “and I decreed death on Adam the first man, to demonstrate that he was human and not a god. § The Gemara returns to the aforementioned verse: “And the Lord will create over the whole habitation of Mount Zion, and over those who are invited to it, a cloud and smoke by day” (Isaiah 4:5). What is the meaning of the phrase: “And over those who are invited to it”? Rabba says that Rabbi Yoḥanan says: Jerusalem of the World-to-Come is not like Jerusalem of this world. With regard to Jerusalem of this world, anyone who wants to ascend there can ascend. With regard to Jerusalem of the World-to-Come, only those who are invited to it can ascend.…”

english_source_translation: Megillah 18a: ““Afterward the children of Israel shall return, and seek the Lord their God and David their king” (Hosea 3:5), and consequently, the blessing of the kingdom of David follows the blessing of the building of Jerusalem. And once the scion of David comes, the time for prayer will come, as it is stated: “I will bring them to My sacred mountain and make them joyful in My house of prayer” (Isaiah 56:7). Therefore, the blessing of hearing prayer is recited after the blessing of the kingdom of David. And after prayer comes, the Temple service will arrive, as it is stated in the continuation of that verse: “Their burnt-offerings and their sacrifices shall be accepted on My altar” (Isaiah 56:7). The blessing of restoration of the Temple service follows the blessing of hearing prayer.…”

english_source_translation: Shemot Rabbah 8:1: “'Who is this King of glory?' (Psalms 24:8)—why is the Holy One, blessed be He, called the King of glory? Because He shares His glory with those who fear Him: a king of flesh and blood does not permit others to ride his horse, sit upon his throne, use his scepter, or wear his crown; yet the Holy One seated Solomon upon His throne ('And Solomon sat on the throne of the Lord as king'), caused Elijah to ride His whirlwind, delivered His staff to Moses, and clothes the King Messiah with His crown.”
kisvei_rav_tzadok_parallel: Kisvei Rav Tzadok Parallel — Dover Tzedek, Miscellany 4:131: “And behold, our Sages stated: "A generation is never less than sixty myriads (600,000)," because the Torah is the underlying blueprint of the universe, and it is known that the 600,000 letters of the Torah are the spiritual roots for the 600,000 primary souls of Israel, and of necessity this must be so in every generation, since the preservation of the entire universe in each era depends solely upon the Torah.…” In Dover Tzedek, Miscellany 4:131 (sharing the proof-text I Chronicles 4:23), Rav Tzadok develops the complementary dimension of this principle, illuminating how Shemot Rabbah 8:1 anchors the inner service of the heart in Sefer HaZikhronot.

english_source_translation: Bereshit Rabbah 8: ““And God said: Let us make Man in our image, in our likeness, and let them dominate over the fish of the sea, and over the birds of the heavens, and over the animals, and over all the earth, and over every crawling creature that crawls upon the earth” (Genesis 1:26). “And God said: Let us make Man in our image, in our likeness.” Rabbi Yoḥanan began: “Back and front [aḥor vakedem], You shaped me…” (Psalms 139:5) – Rabbi Yoḥanan said: If a person merits, he partakes of two worlds, as it is stated: “Back and front, You shaped me.” can be translated “the end, and that which precedes it,” – an allusion to this world and the World to Come. But if not, he will come to give an accounting, as it is stated: “You placed Your palm on me” (Psalms 139:5).).…”

kisvei_rav_tzadok_parallel: Kisvei Rav Tzadok Parallel — Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Dover Tzedek, Berakhot 3:52: “And Elijah embodies the angel of peace, as taught at the end of Eduyot; and as taught that Elijah is Pinchas (Bava Metzia 114b; Zohar III, 215a), concerning whom it is said: "Behold, I give unto him My covenant of peace," for which reason he will herald the final Redemption. english_source_translation: Bereshit Rabbah 27: ““The Lord saw that the wickedness of man was great on the earth, and every inclination of the thoughts of his heart was only evil all the day” (Genesis 6:5). “The Lord saw that the wickedness of man was great” – it is written: “For there is a man whose work is with wisdom, with knowledge, and with smoothness” (Ecclesiastes 2:21). Rabbi Yudan said: How great is the power of prophets, in that they can liken the creation to its Creator, as it is stated, [describing a vision of God]: “I heard the voice of a man by the Ulai” (Daniel 8:16). english_source_translation: Mishneh Torah, Repentance 3: “Each and every person has merits and sins. A person whose merits exceed his sins is [termed] righteous. A person whose sins exceed his merits is [termed] wicked. If [his sins and merits] are equal, he is termed a Beinoni.The same applies to an entire country. If the merits of all its inhabitants exceed their sins, it is [termed] righteous. If their sins are greater, it is [termed] wicked. The same applies to the entire world. If a person's sins exceed his merits, he will immediately die because of his wickedness as [Jeremiah 30:14] states: "[I have smitten you...] for the multitude of your transgressions."Similarly, a country whose sins are great will immediately be obliterated as implied by [Genesis 18:20]: "The outcry of Sodom and Amorah is great....…”

kisvei_ishbitz_radzin_parallel: Kisvei Beis Ishbitz–Radzin Parallel — Beit Yaakov on Torah, Bereshit 10:6: ““The power of His works”—this refers to the deep foundations of the earth,” This teaching from the Ishbitz–Radzin school in Beit Yaakov on Torah, Bereshit 10:6 supplies the foundational Chassidic lens through which Rav Tzadok frames Deuteronomy 4 in Sefer HaZikhronot.

english_source_translation: Mekhilta d'Rabbi Yishmael, Shirata 3 (on Exodus 15:2): “'This is my God, and I will glorify Him': Rabbi Eliezer says: From where do you say that a simple handmaid saw at the Sea what Isaiah and Ezekiel did not see? As it is stated: 'And through the prophets I have used similitudes' (Hosea 12:11).”
kisvei_rav_tzadok_parallel: Kisvei Rav Tzadok Parallel — Divrei Soferim 13:1: “The primary labor of man in this world is the fear of Heaven (yirat Shamayim), which is the treasury and gateway through which all Torah wisdom is preserved in the heart.” This parallel in Divrei Soferim 13:1 directly reinforces Rav Tzadok's exposition here regarding fear of Heaven as the prerequisite and vessel for true Torah knowledge.

english_source_translation: Teshuvot Bayit Chadash, HaYeshanot 5: “Primary source background in Teshuvot Bayit Chadash, HaYeshanot 5 illuminating Rav Tzadok's teaching in this passage.”
kisvei_rav_tzadok_parallel: Kisvei Rav Tzadok Parallel — Takanat HaShavin 15:51: “And on Yom Kippur the complete severance occurs, after which "and Jacob journeyed to Succoth" (Bereishis 33:17), holding the spear (bayin, the lulav) in his hand to proclaim that he has triumphed [Vayikra Rabbah 30:2]; and they dispatch the iniquities to the locus of the root of evil, for everything originated from there, from the yeast in the dough; and Israel remain entirely pure like the ministering angels; and therefore at that time the Satan has no permission to prosecut…” In Takanat HaShavin 15:51 (sharing the proof-text Pirkei DeRabbi Eliezer 46), Rav Tzadok develops the complementary dimension of this principle, illuminating how Teshuvot Bayit Chadash, HaYeshanot 5 anchors the inner service of the heart in Sefer HaZikhronot.
kisvei_ishbitz_radzin_parallel_ref: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Lech Lecha 1
kisvei_ishbitz_radzin_parallel: Kisvei Beis Ishbitz–Radzin Parallel — Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Lech Lecha 1: “'Go for yourself from your land, from your birthplace, and from your father's house' (Genesis 12:1): a person must continually strip away habitual assumptions and natural reliances so as to walk solely by the living illumination of God's word in the present moment.” This foundational Ishbitz–Radzin teaching in Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Lech Lecha 1 illuminates the Mei HaShiloach's teaching on transcending habitual nature through living faith underlying Rav Tzadok's thought.

english_source_translation: Shabbat 92b: “And if you say that the people of Hotzal do so and therefore they should be liable, their intention is rendered irrelevant by the opinions of all other people. MISHNA: One who intends to carry out an object with the object before him, and as he was walking the object came to be carried behind him, is exempt. However, if he intended to carry it out behind him and it came to be carried before him, he is liable. In truth they said: A woman who girded herself in a pants-like sinar worn beneath the outer garments, whether she placed an object before her or behind her, and it came to be carried on the other side, she is liable, as it is common for the sinar to be reversed.…”
kisvei_rav_tzadok_parallel: Kisvei Rav Tzadok Parallel — Likkutei Maamarim, On Shimshon 7: “And the overarching principle is: that the depth of the concealed divine Will enclothes itself in letters and words, which serve as a vessel to contract it, so that the will is formulated according to the letters and words; each letter being a 'stone', and each word is a 'house' and complete vessel to receive the light of the will alluded to in that word.…” In Likkutei Maamarim, On Shimshon 7 (sharing the proof-text Shemot Rabbah 41), Rav Tzadok develops the complementary dimension of this principle, illuminating how Shabbat 92b anchors the inner service of the heart in Sefer HaZikhronot.
kisvei_ishbitz_radzin_parallel: Kisvei Beis Ishbitz–Radzin Parallel — Beit Yaakov on Torah, Noach 52:84: “Fulfilling Habakkuk 2:4, 'The righteous shall live by his faith': true life consists of recognizing that all human strength and wisdom flow moment by moment from the Creator alone.” This foundational Ishbitz–Radzin teaching in Beit Yaakov on Torah, Noach 52:84 illuminates living by emunah as the single foundation of all the commandments underlying Rav Tzadok's thought.

english_source_translation: Shemot Rabbah 41: ““He gave to Moses, as He concluded speaking with him on Mount Sinai, the two tablets of Testimony, stone tablets, written with the finger of God” (Exodus 31:18). “He gave to Moses, as He concluded.” Rabbi Tanḥuma bar Abba began in this way: “With You, Lord, is the righteousness, and with us the shame” (Daniel 9:7). What is the reason that this is so? Rabbi Neḥemya said: Even when we are performing acts of righteousness, we look at our actions and we experience shame. There is no time that we come with demands, other than when we are taking out our tithes, as it is stated: “When you conclude tithing” (Deuteronomy 26:12). What is written at the end? “Look from Your holy abode, from the heavens, [and bless Your people Israel, and the land that You gave us]” (Deuteronomy 26:15). 9a) (Maharzu).…”
kisvei_rav_tzadok_parallel_ref: Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 8:2
kisvei_rav_tzadok_parallel: Kisvei Rav Tzadok Parallel — Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 8:2: “However, although "turn from evil" precedes, the primary focus is "do good" Psalms 34:15, and "I am Hashem" precedes "You shall have no other gods," accomplished through the light of Torah. And these are the forty-nine days of the Omer following the Exodus, refining the 49 Gates of Understanding in good, meriting the Fiftieth Gate on Shavuot, becoming free from the Angel of Death and the evil inclination (Shemot Rabbah 41:7), which was the purification of the root, the crowns…” In Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 8:2 (sharing the proof-text Shemot Rabbah 41, Chagigah 11b), Rav Tzadok develops the complementary dimension of this principle, illuminating how Shemot Rabbah 41 anchors the inner service of the heart in Sefer HaZikhronot.

kisvei_ishbitz_radzin_parallel: Kisvei Beis Ishbitz–Radzin Parallel — Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 8:5: “And from this it is perceived that Hashem is God, there is none else beside Him; for should it enter man's thought, Heaven forbid, that there are two sovereign powers, if so, how could one encroach into the boundary of the other?!
